findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script into build shell
findings.whyItBreaks: The added layer runs `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh`, executing arbitrary remote content as root during the image build with no integrity or provenance check. The script is fetched at build time from an unpinned URL and is not verified by checksum, signature, or version pin, so whoever controls that endpoint (or the content itself changing over time) gets arbitrary code execution baked into every build of this image. The `-sL` flags make it worse: `-s` silences curl errors and there is no `--fail`/`-f`, so an HTTP 4xx/5xx error page (or empty/redirected body) is still piped into `sh` and executed, and because a pipeline's exit status is that of `sh` (no `set -o pipefail`), a failed download is not surfaced — the build can succeed having executed a failure body. This is an unverified third-party code execution surface introduced by this PR.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating failure with a real value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load (src/store.go:7) deliberately returns the sentinel ErrMissing to distinguish 'key absent' from 'key present with empty value'. The new helper does `v, _ := Load(key, m)` (src/store.go:16), discarding that signal. Result: `LoadOrDefault("missing", map[string]string{"k":""})` and `LoadOrDefault("k", map[string]string{"k":""})` both return ""; every caller is forced to conflate a lookup failure with a legitimate empty value, and any code that later persists, reports, or acts on the returned string cannot tell the two apart. No in-repo caller exists yet, but this is an exported API contract shipping now.

findings.title: worker.Run now emits results out of order via unbounded goroutines
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, Run sent results[j]*2 in input order (blocking send per iteration), so a consumer could pair each received value with jobs[i] positionally and would observe at most one in-flight send. Now each iteration launches an independent goroutine that races to send on the shared unbuffered channel, so delivery order is scheduler-dependent and arbitrary. Any consumer that relies on positional correspondence (the natural contract of a `jobs []int` -> `results chan int` fan-out API) receives the correct multiset of values but attached to the wrong job index. The change also removes the implicit backpressure: the old code serialized sends inside the caller's loop, while the new code spawns len(jobs) goroutines up front, all of which block on `results <-` if the receiver drains slowly or stops early, leaking goroutines for the process lifetime. The `context.Context` parameter is still ignored, so nothing bounds or cancels this fan-out.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord OR lets admins delete across tenants and any user delete others' records
findings.whyItBreaks: The base guard `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` required BOTH admin rights and tenant match. With `||`, the tenant check no longer constrains admins: an admin whose session.tenantId is 'A' now returns true for a record whose tenantId is 'B', enabling cross-tenant deletion. Symmetrically, a non-admin whose tenantId equals the record's tenantId now returns true, so any regular user can delete any record in their tenant regardless of record.ownerId. Both are access-control bypasses on a destructive path (data loss).

findings.title: parseSettings now swallows parse/validation errors and returns DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change a malformed JSON payload or an invalid theme/fontSize threw out of parseSettings (base src/settings.ts:9-11), so updateFontSize aborted before saving and the error was visible to the caller. Now the catch-all discards the JSON syntax error and the explicit "bad theme"/"bad fontSize" validations and returns { theme: "light", fontSize: 14 }. The in-repo caller updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) cannot distinguish failure from a legitimate value: it mutates the returned fallback and calls save(), overwriting the user's persisted settings with defaults plus the new size, silently destroying the stored theme/other fields that were previously left intact, and no error is ever surfaced. Because parseSettings is exported, every external caller is also forced to conflate corruption with a real default value.

findings.title: Revert Math.floor: pageCount drops the final partial page
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount must return the number of pages needed to hold totalItems. With Math.floor, any totalItems not an exact multiple of pageSize under-reports by one: e.g. totalItems=11, pageSize=10 → returns 1, but 11 items require 2 pages; totalItems=1, pageSize=10 → returns 0. Callers that iterate pages or size pagination off this value will omit the last partial page (the tail items are never displayed/processed). The previous Math.ceil was correct here.

facts.meaning: The page count rounds down instead of up.
A remainder/partial final page is omitted or a small result becomes zero pages.

findings.title: Artifacts fetched from 'verified' ref, not the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior was self-consistent: `builtFrom` and the artifact list both came from `build.ref(branch)`. The change adds `const verified = build.ref("verified")` and uses `build.artifactsAt(verified)` while still setting `builtFrom: commit` (the branch ref). For any `branch` whose ref does not resolve to the same commit as the fixed ref named "verified", the returned BuildReport lists `builtFrom` = branch commit but `artifacts` = artifacts of the "verified" ref, i.e. artifacts that were not produced from the commit the report claims. This is wrong reported data, and the hardcoded "verified" ref also silently ignores the `branch` argument for artifact selection.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores `limit`, returns unbounded entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The function's carrier still promises 'Returns at most `limit` entries' (src/feed.ts:1) but the body now returns the full reversed array with no `.slice(0, limit)`. The new `if (limit <= 0) return [];` only clamps the non-positive case. The relying caller renderFeed calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` (src/feed.ts:9-11) and sizes `out` at 20: `const out = new Array<string>(20); for (let i = 0; i < page.length; i++) out[i] = page[i];`. With page.length > 20 the loop writes past index 19, and in JS assigning an index beyond length extends the array, so renderFeed returns >20 entries (feeds of any real length regress from a 20-item page to the entire list).

findings.title: monthRange end shifted to last-day 00:00 drops last day of month from revenue
findings.whyItBreaks: end is now Date.UTC(year, month, 0) = 00:00 of the month's LAST day (e.g. monthRange(2026,1).end = 2026-01-31T00:00Z; previously Date.UTC(2026,1,1) = 2026-02-01T00:00Z). contains() is still end-exclusive: t >= start && t < end (src/lib/date-range.ts:32). So for every month the window is [first-day 00:00, last-day 00:00) and all invoices issued on the last calendar day (even exactly 00:00) fail the predicate and are excluded. monthlyRevenue() feeds this range straight into contains(range, inv.issuedAt) at src/reports/monthly.ts:17, so invoiceCount/totalCents under-report, and the error propagates through monthlyCsv() at src/reports/export.ts:5 into exported CSV money totals. The predicate correctly rejects a value, but the rejected invoices are legitimately in-month, making this a regression, not a tightening.

facts.meaning: monthRange's end is now day 0 of the following month (the requested month's last day at midnight) instead of the first day of the next month.
Records on the last day of a month fall outside the half-open range and are omitted from monthly totals.

findings.title: Header entry-count no longer matches emitted rows after stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now emits only non-stale rows (`live`), but `headerLines(opts, entries.length)` still passes the total entry count. For any input containing `stale: true` entries the output self-contradicts: the `# entry-count: N` header reports N while only `live.length < N` rows follow. Any consumer that trusts `entry-count` (integrity checks, sizing/paging, reconciliation against its own index) is now fed a wrong value, and it is wrong only when stale entries exist — exactly the case this change was made to handle.

findings.title: Restore execute() — it now unconditionally throws
findings.whyItBreaks: Base implementation returned input.toUpperCase() (verified via git show 9a6ca65:src/runner.ts). The changed line replaces it with `throw new Error("always fails")`, so every invocation of the module's only export throws instead of returning a value. The unchanged signature still advertises `(input: string) => string`, so any consumer that relied on the returned string now receives an exception on every call — a direct user-facing regression of the exported contract.

findings.title: Viewer check in isEligible makes handle's read-only path unreachable
findings.whyItBreaks: `isEligible` now returns false for every `role === "viewer"` request (src/handler.ts:18), but the only caller, `handle`, runs `if (!isEligible(req)) return "rejected"` (src/handler.ts:24) before its `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only"` branch (src/handler.ts:25). Substituting a viewer request (e.g. {status:"active",role:"viewer",attempts:0}): previously isEligible returned true and handle returned "read-only"; now isEligible returns false and handle returns "rejected", so line 25 is dead code. This is TRIGGER A over-block: the eligibility predicate does not legitimately govern the role-based read-only action — base code deliberately treated viewers as eligible-but-read-only — so the change rejects an action that was legitimately approvable on its own and breaks the viewer workflow.

findings.title: Shared canProceed now blocks saving drafts until paid
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed gates two distinct actions. src/actions.ts:4 submitOrder legitimately depends on payment, but src/actions.ts:9 saveDraft does not. After this change, saveDraft(order{state:"draft",payment:"missing"}) evaluates canProceed -> false and returns "blocked" instead of "saved", so a user can no longer save an unpaid draft. Substituting payment="missing": guard `order.payment === "paid"` @src/policy.ts:7 rejects -> canProceed false -> saveDraft returns "blocked" (previously "saved").

findings.title: publishSnapshot returns files from "stable" instead of the requested channel
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot's commit is repo.headCommit(channel) (line 13) but its files are now repo.filesAt(stable) (line 14/18), where stable = repo.headCommit("stable"). For any channel other than stable, files[] no longer describes the commit it is paired with: a caller publishing channel "main" (or any feature channel) receives a Snapshot whose commit points at one tree while files lists another ref's contents. The unchanged body makes the contrary promise — the parameter is named channel and the original code used repo.filesAt(head) — so this is a wrong-value substitution on a live, exported path (every call site is affected, none are legitimately served by stable's files).

findings.title: Unused `limit` param: body ignores it, returns 10 items regardless
findings.whyItBreaks: `build` now advertises `build(prefix, limit=10)`, so any caller passing `limit=N` expects at most N results (capping is an observable output property). The body never reads `limit`: line 2 still hardcodes `max_count = 10` and the loop appends `max_count` items. `build('x', limit=3)` therefore returns 10 items, violating the signature's contract. This is an exported/public carrier whose promised behavior (capping) affects the result a caller receives, so it is a defect even before any in-repo caller exists.

findings.title: parse_positive_int name promises positivity but body accepts non-positive values
findings.whyItBreaks: The public symbol was renamed from read_int to parse_positive_int, promising that the input is validated as a positive integer, but the body is unchanged (`return int(value)`). It still accepts negative and zero values without error (e.g. parse_positive_int(-5) returns -5, parse_positive_int("0") returns 0), so any caller trusting the name and relying on a strictly positive result gets a non-positive value instead of a validation error. The promised validation materially affects the value a caller receives.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation built `result = df.copy()`, applied assignments to the copy, and returned it, so the caller's `df` was left untouched. The head version writes directly into the passed-in frame (`df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value`) and returns that same object. Any caller holding a reference to the original frame (e.g. reusing it for a baseline/undo, comparing before/after, or sharing it across calls) now observes its `value` column silently overwritten. Because the function also returns the same object it mutated, the aliasing is invisible: `out = apply_values(df, m)` and `df` are identical, so callers cannot even detect the side effect.

findings.title: Moving ci.yml to docs/ci.md disables CI entirely
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub Actions only discovers workflow files under .github/workflows/. This rename (R100) leaves no YAML under .github/workflows/ (the .github directory no longer exists), so 'push'/'pull_request' triggers never run `npm ci`, `npm run lint`, or `npm test`. Every push/PR loses its CI gate, and README.md:5 ('CI runs lint and tests on every push') becomes false — the removed path was the only workflow in the repo.

findings.title: Remove leftover dbg! that leaks inputs to stderr
findings.whyItBreaks: `process` is a public function and `dbg!(items)` unconditionally writes the full `items` vector (including any sensitive/PII payload the caller passes) to stderr on every invocation, and also makes the crate emit debug noise in production. This is debug scaffolding committed to a shipping code path, not intended behavior.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against fromRevision, not latest
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset interface documents fromRevision as "Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision" (src/changeset.ts:7-8). The changed line computes changedPaths from store.resolve("latest") while fromRevision is still store.resolve(pinnedTag), so the two halves of the returned Changeset now describe different bases. Any consumer that replays the paths on top of fromRevision (the only revision it is given) applies changes derived from the tip of the history onto the pinned revision, producing wrong file contents/conflicts, and the pinned-tag diff that callers asked for is silently replaced by the latest diff. The mismatch is invisible to a type checker because both values are strings.

findings.title: Update consumer query after renaming users.email to contact_email
findings.whyItBreaks: migrations/0002_rename.sql:1 renames the users column email -> contact_email, but the only query in the repo still reads the old name: src/query.sql:1 is `SELECT email FROM users`. After 0002 is applied the column email no longer exists, so that query fails with an unknown-column error, breaking the repo's sole data path. Nothing in the tree references contact_email (`rg -n "contact_email" .` returns only the migration), so the rename is not accompanied by any consumer update.

findings.title: Hardcoded live billing API key committed to source
findings.whyItBreaks: makeClient() is exported and now returns the literal credential `bk_live_9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0` for every caller instead of reading BILLING_API_KEY from the environment. A secret baked into version control is exposed to anyone with repo/artifact access, cannot be rotated without a code change, and ships to every build/consumer — a credential leak with direct billing impact.

findings.title: Missing-key guard removed; failure now silently yields a default value
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously an unset BILLING_API_KEY raised `throw new Error("BILLING_API_KEY is not set")`, so callers could distinguish 'not configured' from 'configured'. The changed body discards that failure signal and returns a plausible-looking string instead; makeClient() is an exported public path, so every caller is now forced to conflate misconfiguration (auth failures, requests billed against an unintended key) with a legitimately configured client, and no in-repo caller can detect the difference.

findings.title: Inverted isAdmin guard lets non-admins purge projects
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required `user.isAdmin && project.archived` to purge. The new guard returns "forbidden" when `user.isAdmin` is true, so control only reaches `db.delete(project.id)` (line 14) for a NON-admin user whose project is archived. An ordinary non-privileged user can therefore delete (purge) an archived project, an authorization bypass leading to data loss; simultaneously admins are always rejected.

facts.meaning: The refactored guard incorrectly returns forbidden for administrators.
Non-administrators can reach the destructive project purge/delete path.
The refactored guard incorrectly returns forbidden for administrators.

findings.title: Restore guard for load_settings() returning None before subscripting
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() still returns None when the path does not exist (app/config.py:7-8). The deleted lines were exactly the guard for that sentinel. After the change, startup() does settings = load_settings(path) then int(settings["workers"]); when the file is absent, settings is None and None["workers"] raises TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable. The previous behavior (base e5f259e) returned int(1) via the {"workers": 1} default, so this is a behavior regression on the missing-file path: a missing config now aborts startup with an obscure TypeError rather than a defined/clear result.

findings.title: Charge discards gateway error and reports success
findings.whyItBreaks: gw.Submit's error was previously propagated via fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err). The changed code only logs it and falls through to `return nil`, so every caller of the exported Charge sees a successful result for a failed charge. Failure and success are now indistinguishable at the API boundary, so callers can mark an order paid, ship goods, or issue a receipt for money that was never captured.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, serving one tenant's setting to another
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the key was `${tenantId}:${name}`; now `cacheKey(name)` yields `settings:${name}`, which has no tenant component, and the value stored is the result of `store.fetch(tenantId, name)` for whichever tenant populated the entry first. Call `settingsFor('tenantB', 'x', store)` after `settingsFor('tenantA', 'x', store)` and the cache hit at line 14 returns tenantA's value without ever calling `store.fetch('tenantB', 'x')`. Cross-tenant value leakage plus wrong settings for the second tenant — a tenant-scoping security/correctness defect, not a mere cache miss.

findings.title: invalidate() drops tenantId, breaking scoped eviction
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature changed from `invalidate(tenantId, name)` to `invalidate(name)` and deletes `settings:${name}`. Any existing caller that invalidated a single tenant's entry (e.g. after that tenant updated a setting) now either fails to compile (two args against the one-arg signature) or, if recompiled, never evicts the stale per-tenant value because the key it deletes no longer corresponds to the tenant that was updated. Combined with the tenant-agnostic key at line 12, tenant-specific invalidation is impossible.

findings.title: Async reserve creates oversell race between await and in-memory decrement
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve now awaits store.save (line 17) before mutating this.stock (line 18). Because the yield point sits between the read of `remaining` (line 15) and the local decrement, two concurrent reserve(sku) calls both compute the same `remaining`, both pass the `remaining <= 0` guard, and both call save(sku, remaining-1). Concrete: with stock loaded to 1, two overlapping calls both resolve true, the store is written 0, and this.stock ends at 0 — two reservations honored for one unit (lost update / oversell). In the base revision reserve was synchronous with no yield point, so this interleaving was impossible; the change is what introduces it.

findings.title: backoff() unit change to ms not propagated; retry sleeps 1000x too long
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff now returns milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2 ** attempt * 1000)); schedulePoll was updated to pass it straight to setTimeout, but the other consumer src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. That multiplies milliseconds by 1000 again: attempt 0 yields 1000 * 1000 = 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min), and the capped case yields 30_000 * 1000 = 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 hours) per retry. A job that previously backed off 1s/2s/4s now stalls for minutes to hours, effectively breaking the retry path.

findings.title: Save drops f.Close() error, reporting false success on failed writes
findings.whyItBreaks: OLD code ended with `return f.Close()`, so a close-time error (delayed writeback failure on network/overlay/FUSE filesystems, ENOSPC surfaced at close, etc.) was returned to the caller. NEW code uses `defer f.Close()`, which discards that error, and `Save` now returns only `w.Flush()`. bufio.Flush only pushes bytes into the kernel/file; durability errors that surface at close are no longer observable. Because `Save` is an exported public API, every caller that treats a nil return as "saved" will now report/advance state as though the write succeeded when it may not have — silent data loss with no distinguishable failure signal.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of each page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end), but page_window iterates range(start, end - 1) instead of range(start, end). The final row of every non-empty page is silently omitted. Concretely, rows=[a,b,c,d,e] with page_size=2: page 0 originally returned [a,b], now returns [a]; with page_size=1 every page returns [] because range(start, start) is empty. render_page (line 40) consumes this window, so summarize (line 52) emits pages missing their last row (or entirely empty pages for size 1), a user-visible pagination regression versus the base implementation's range(start, end).

findings.title: TtlCache.get serves expired values and drops fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was inverted. With `age > ttlMs` returning entry.value, an entry older than the TTL is treated as valid, so callers receive stale/expired data forever; the subsequent `delete(key)` + `return null` branch now executes for FRESH entries only, so every lookup misses within the TTL window. Net effect: the cache always misses when it should hit and always hits when it should miss — a correctness regression for all consumers of get().

findings.title: pruneDone skips consecutive done jobs and mutates caller array
findings.whyItBreaks: splice during forEach shifts remaining elements down while forEach advances the index, so any done job immediately following a removed one is skipped. Substitute jobs=[{done:true},{done:true}]: index 0 done -> splice -> array becomes [{done:true}]; forEach next index 1 is out of range -> loop ends, leaving a done job in the result. The returned array still contains done jobs that pruneDone is supposed to remove. Second regression: the change also mutates the caller's input array in place (previously `filter` returned a new array), so callers observing their original array now see it altered.

findings.title: averageAmount([]) now returns NaN instead of 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard was removed, so an empty input reaches `total / rows.length` = 0 / 0 = NaN. This is a behavior change for the exported public function: callers that relied on the documented-by-behavior empty result of 0 now receive NaN, which propagates silently through any arithmetic or display and is not an obvious error.

findings.title: busiest mutates the caller's array via in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: The defensive copy `[...rows]` was removed, so `rows.sort(...)` reorders the caller's own array as a side effect. Callers who pass an array and continue using it after calling `busiest` (e.g. re-reading it, iterating it again, or persisting it) now observe it silently reordered by amount; `busiest`'s job is only to report the max, so this is unexpected mutation of caller-owned data.

findings.title: Restore numeric sort so cutoff picks the correct Nth-highest score
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort() with no comparator coerces scores to strings and orders them lexicographically (by UTF-16 code units), then reverse() yields lexicographic-descending, not numeric-descending. Line 15 uses scores[min(n,len)-1] as the threshold for filter, so a wrong ordering yields a wrong cutoff and topPlayers returns the wrong set of players. Example: players with scores [1, 10, 2] and n=2 — default sort gives [1,10,2], reverse gives [2,10,1], cutoff = scores[1] = 10, filter keeps only score>=10 → returns just [10], dropping score 2 (the true 2nd place). The old comparator (b - a) produced [10,2,1], cutoff 2 → [10,2].

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation compared the computed HMAC against the caller-supplied signature with hmac.compare_digest, which runs in time independent of how many leading bytes match. The new line uses Python's `==` on `str`, which short-circuits at the first differing character, so comparison time grows with the number of matching leading hex digits. An attacker who can submit webhook payloads and observe response latency (the 401 vs 200 branch in handle() at app/webhook.py:14-16, which calls processor()) can recover the expected signature one hex digit at a time and then forge a signature that passes verify() and reaches processor(payload). The boolean accept/reject result for a fully-correct signature is unchanged, which is exactly why this defect is invisible to functional tests.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, the ledger insert, the debit, and the credit all ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block (base 54fdbf1 app/transfer.py:4-16). The head only wraps `_record_ledger` in the transaction (app/transfer.py:22-23) and calls `_apply_balances` after it, at app/transfer.py:24, i.e. after the block has committed. The ledger row now commits separately from the balance changes, and the two balance UPDATEs are also no longer atomic with each other. If `_apply_balances` fails or the process dies after the commit (e.g. credit fails after debit, or crash between the two UPDATEs), the ledger entry is persisted with no/partial balance movement: money is destroyed (debit applied, credit not) or created, and ledger/balances permanently diverge. The atomicity guarantee held on every call before this change and is now lost on every call.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time instead of UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor replaces the UTC accessors getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate with the local-time accessors getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. The result of billingDay(at) is now a function of the host's TZ, not just the instant: the same Date maps to different billing-day strings across environments (dev/test/prod, containers with TZ=UTC vs a host TZ), and any instant within the local-midnight window returns a day that differs by ±1 from the previous UTC behavior. Because billingDay is exported and sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8) delegates to it, day-equality/attribution decisions shift by a full day near midnight, which can mis-attribute charges to the wrong billing day and break day-based idempotency/dedup.

findings.title: Cache key dropped tenant, causing cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `memo` (line 7) is shared across all calls. Previously the key was `${tenant}:${account}`, keeping entries tenant-scoped. Now the key is only `account`, so the first call for (tenantA, 'alice') stores Profile{tenant:'tenantA'} under 'alice', and a later call for (tenantB, 'alice') hits `memo.get('alice')` at line 15, returns the cached tenantA profile at line 16, and never calls fetchProfile(tenantB, 'alice'). The returned Profile carries the wrong `tenant` and `displayName`, i.e. cross-tenant data disclosure plus incorrect profile data.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version of load() propagated `Error('missing: <key>')` so callers could detect an absent key. The new catch-all converts every failure into "", which is a valid Map<string,string> value (a stored empty string is indistinguishable from a missing key). loadAll (src/store.ts:12) maps load over keys and will silently splice "" into its result array for missing keys, so downstream consumers get a plausible-but-wrong value instead of an error. load() is an exported/public contract, so every caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Field reads value.length on string|number, breaking number values
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value was widened to `string | number` (line 2), but the body immediately accesses `value.length`. Under TypeScript's union property-access rules this is a compile error (TS2339: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'), so the build/typecheck fails for any caller passing a number. Even ignoring TS, at runtime `(42).length` is `undefined`, so the input's defaultValue becomes the literal string `len=undefined` instead of a length, silently mislabeling the field.

findings.title: Do not echo secrets.TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step injects the repository secret `secrets.TOKEN` into the environment and then prints it with `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`. This writes the deploy credential into the workflow run log, which is readable by anyone with repo/log access and is commonly exported or shipped to log aggregators. GitHub's log masking only best-effort replaces exact registered values and does not protect derived/transformed output or logs pulled outside the masking path, so the secret should never be printed. The workflow runs `on: push` for every branch, multiplying the exposure opportunities.

findings.title: Restore 64 MiB maxBuffer on git() to avoid ENOBUFS on large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer falls back to spawnSync's default of 1024*1024 (1 MiB). git() produces the full-PR patch at line 140 (`git diff mergeBase headSha`); when that output exceeds 1 MiB, spawnSync returns res.error=ENOBUFS with status null, so the `res.status !== 0` check at line 38 throws "git diff ... failed:" (empty stderr) and the entire review aborts. The sibling helpers still set 64 MiB (gh at line 19, ghText at line 29), showing the guard was deliberate.

findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox in runCodex args
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `-s read-only` was the only guarantee that the spawned `codex exec` runs read-only. CLI `--sandbox` overrides config, so with the flag present the mode was pinned read-only; without it, sandbox mode is resolved from `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` (and trusted project config). Codex's built-in default is read-only (official docs: "By default, codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox"), so a bare default config is unchanged — but any host where `sandbox_mode` is set to `workspace-write`/`danger-full-access` (a normal interactive/dev setting) now runs this subprocess with write/exec access while `spawnSync` points it at `opts.repoPath` (src/shared/codex.ts:23), i.e. the untrusted repository under review. That silently widens the injection/write surface the runner previously closed.

findings.title: Restore merge-base so the reviewed diff excludes base-branch changes
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code computed mergeBase = git merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and diffed mergeBase..headSha (the PR-only change set). The new code endpoint-diffs baseSha directly against the local HEAD, which is NOT the PR-only change set unless baseSha happens to be an ancestor of HEAD. Concretely, with the common config `pull_request.base.sha` set into PR_BASE_SHA and checkout of the PR head ref, baseSha is the base-branch tip at event time while the PR head forked earlier, so git merge-base(baseSha, headSha) != baseSha: `git diff baseSha HEAD` then renders every base-branch commit merged after the fork as reverse deletions in the patch and lists those files in changedFiles/changedPaths. The reviewer (src/adapters/github.ts:167) is fed that polluted patch, and inlineComments (src/adapters/github.ts:63) filters on the over-inclusive changedPaths set. The diff also no longer uses headSha/PR_HEAD_SHA at all (it silently became dead for the patch while still used as the review commit_id at src/adapters/github.ts:178), so the reviewed content and the reported commit can diverge.

findings.title: Plain-string replace interprets $ patterns, corrupting prompt payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: `String.prototype.replace` applies special replacement patterns ($$, $&, $`, $', $n) when replaceValue is a string, but uses the function's return value verbatim when replaceValue is a function. The base revision deliberately passed `() => JSON.stringify(...)` (and `() => bundle.patch`) to avoid this interpretation; the diff removes those wrappers. `bundle.patch` is an arbitrary unified diff and the serialized bundle contains arbitrary repo text, so any occurrence of these sequences is rewritten: `$$` collapses to a single `$`, `$&` re-injects the literal placeholder (e.g. `{{PATCH}}`) instead of the content, `$'` injects the prompt tail after the match, `` $` `` injects the prompt head. The model then receives a silently corrupted patch/bundle, producing wrong reviews with no error surfaced.

findings.title: Restore commit_id in fallback review create to pin it to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview's primary call (lines 88-99) sends commit_id=headSha, but the catch fallback (lines 101-113, taken whenever the --input create fails, e.g. inline-comment line positions rejected at 422) now omits commit_id. GitHub's POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{number}/reviews defaults commit_id to the PR's most recent commit, so if the branch advanced after headSha was captured (PR_HEAD_SHA at line 141), the fallback review is attached to an unreviewed commit. It also diverges from postCheck (line 184), which still posts the check run against headSha, so the review verdict and the check run can reference different commits.

findings.title: Restore finding validation: normalizeFinding now fabricates defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Base normalizeFinding threw on malformed input and normalizeReview(raw, strict=true) propagated that error, so bad model output was rejected loudly. The new body discards every guard and substitutes defaults: severity -> "P1", category -> "bug", title -> "Untitled finding", file -> "", lineStart/lineEnd -> 0 (Number() yields NaN for non-numeric input), whyItBreaks/suggestedFix -> "". Because the exported normalizeReview (line 113/131) also drops its `strict` parameter, callers can no longer distinguish a malformed finding from a real one and will surface a fabricated P1 finding anchored to file "" line 0, violating the review-output contract that each finding cite a concrete changed file and line range.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view in the pre-checkout refs step
findings.whyItBreaks: These are the only lines that run on workflow_dispatch (the pull_request path takes the `-n "$EVENT_HEAD"` branch). Removing `-R "$REPO"` forces gh to resolve the repository itself: gh's BaseRepo uses cmdutil.OverrideBaseRepoFunc, which falls back to `GH_REPO` and otherwise to git remotes read from the current working directory (go-gh repository.Current: GH_REPO else `git remote -v`). The step runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (line 42) and GITHUB_REPOSITORY is not consulted by gh, so on a fresh/cleaned/containerized self-hosted workspace (`_work/<repo>/<repo>` exists but has no .git) `gh pr view` exits non-zero with 'no git remotes found'. That failure is inside `$(...)` passed as an argument to `echo`, so bash -e does not fail the step (verified: `bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail -c 'echo "head=$(false)"; echo done'` prints `head=` and exits 0), and the step reports success with empty `head`/`base`. actions/checkout then receives `ref: ''` and (verified in actions/checkout v4 input-helper.ts:79-90) falls back to github.context.ref/sha — the branch selected in the dispatch UI, not the requested PR head — and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are passed empty to src/cli.ts, so the review silently runs against the wrong revision instead of failing. On a shared/persistent runner whose leftover workspace is a different repository, gh would instead resolve that other repo and return the wrong PR's SHAs.

findings.title: Candidate review parsed leniently silently drops real findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview's second parameter is `strict` (default true); with strict=false it catches per-finding normalization failures and filters those findings out instead of throwing. A candidate finding that is a real defect but has one malformed required field (e.g. non-numeric lineStart/confidence) is dropped, so `candidate.findings` no longer contains it. The critic is prune-only and receives only `{{FINDINGS}}` from `candidate` (line 35), so the dropped finding can never reappear in `pruned`, and deriveVerdict can then return `pass`. Before this change the malformed candidate threw at line 29 and the run failed closed rather than under-reporting.

findings.title: Do not silently default malformed review output to an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw on non-object input and on missing/mistyped summary, findings, checked, and residual_risks. The new body swallows every one of those signals and returns {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]} instead. Because normalizeReview is exported and its declared return type RawReview has no error channel, every caller is now forced to treat 'the model produced garbage / truncated JSON / null' identically to 'a well-formed review that legitimately found nothing'. A downstream verdict step reading this normalized review will see an empty summary and zero findings and can map that to 'pass', whereas the prior behavior surfaced a distinguishable error. This is exactly the swallowed-failure class: the function no longer lets callers distinguish failure from a real value.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch no longer checks out the requested PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow still declares a `workflow_dispatch` trigger (lines 10-14) and the job `if:` (line 24) still admits it, but for `workflow_dispatch` `github.event.pull_request` is null, so every `github.event.pull_request.*` expression below resolves to an empty string. Result: line 29 `ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` falls back to `github.ref` (the branch the run was dispatched from, e.g. `refs/heads/main`) instead of the PR head; lines 45-46 set `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` to empty; line 35 fetches `main` as the base regardless of the PR's real base branch. The removed `Resolve PR refs` step covered exactly this case via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid/baseRefOid/baseRef`, so this is a regression: a manually triggered review now installs/checks out and reviews the default branch rather than the requested PR, and hands the CLI empty base/head SHAs.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git(): 1 MiB default aborts large-diff reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer drops the cap to Node's spawnSync default of 1024 * 1024 bytes. git() reads the full patch via git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd) at src/adapters/local.ts:100, and large PRs (regenerated lockfiles, generated/minified files, vendored code) routinely exceed 1 MiB. On overflow spawnSync returns status=null with error.code=ENOBUFS and truncated stdout (verified: status=null err=ENOBUFS stdoutLen≈1,049,961). The guard at src/adapters/local.ts:12 (`res.status !== 0`) then throws, so the local review fails entirely and prints a misleading `git diff ... failed:` message with empty stderr, instead of the review result. This is a user-facing regression from the base, which set maxBuffer: 64 MiB; the sibling gh() helper still keeps its 64 MiB cap, showing the intent was per-call buffering, not a deliberate removal.

findings.title: Stop downgrading failed review check from failure to neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch path the run posts the 'Needlefish' check-run with conclusion "neutral" (was "failure"). GitHub treats a neutral conclusion as acceptable for required status checks (neutral/skipped/success pass; only failure/cancelled/timed_out/action_required block), so a PR whose review errored out (e.g. gh/git failure thrown from ghText `pr diff` at line 143, or a review-core exception) will no longer be blocked when 'Needlefish' is a required check — an infrastructure/error failure now looks identical to the benign `needs_human` verdict (`VERDICT_CONCLUSION.needs_human = "neutral"` at src/adapters/github.ts:53). This directly contradicts the summary text posted on line 193 ("Review errored and did NOT pass this PR"), so the check's promise and its gate disagree. The process still exits 1 (line 196), but the check-run conclusion is the merge gate.

findings.title: Keep a trusted tool checkout so a PR cannot approve itself
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow's `Checkout trusted tool (main)` step (base lines 51-56) ran the reviewer from trusted `main`, with the PR head only checked out as the read-only target at path `target`. This diff deletes that step and changes `Checkout review target (PR head)` to check out into the workspace root (line 43-47) with no `path`, so `Install` (line 49-51) runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against the PR's own manifest (executing PR-controlled lifecycle scripts) and the review step (line 59) executes the PR-controlled `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` as the reviewer. Because the review step still receives `GH_TOKEN` (line 56) under `permissions: pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` (lines 16-19), a same-repo branch author can rewrite `src/cli.ts` (or a postinstall hook) to always emit PASS or forge check runs, defeating the required review check this workflow exists to provide. The manual `workflow_dispatch` path is worse: the `if:` at line 24 admits dispatch for any PR number, so dispatching a fork PR runs the fork's code with the write-scoped token on the self-hosted runner. The comment at lines 3-5 reframes this as intentional 'self-review mode', but for THIS repo it removes the protection with no replacement (the README template is only for OTHER repos).

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: normalizeFinding no longer coerces severity; "p0"/" p1" fall through to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous body computed const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() and then tested SEVERITIES.includes(sev), so case- and whitespace-variant severities ("p0", " p1 ") normalized to their canonical form. The new body tests SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity) directly, so those same values now fail the membership check and take the fallback branch. Because that fallback also changed from "P1" to "P3", a raw severity of "p0" that used to normalize to P0 is now emitted as P3 — a silent severity downgrade in the exported normalizer that the surrounding code (raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding) at line 132) applies to every finding by default. For a review-gating normalizer, mapping unrecognized input to the lowest severity is fail-open: a real P0/P1 can be persisted and later surfaced as P3.

findings.title: Restore credential scrubbing before spawning codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed block built a copy of process.env with GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN deleted and passed it as `env` to spawnSync. With that deletion dropped, spawnSync falls back to inheriting the parent process.env, so the `codex exec` subprocess — which is driven by a prompt derived from the (untrusted) repository under review — is now handed those credentials. Any prompt-injection in the reviewed content that makes the subprocess read/emit env vars, or any tool the agent invokes, can exfiltrate or misuse the GitHub token that the base revision deliberately withheld. This is a secret-exposure regression on a supply-chain surface, not a style change.

findings.title: Removing fork guard runs untrusted PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control preventing this job from running for fork-originated PRs. Without it, on any `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened) from a fork the job proceeds to check out the fork's `head.sha` (lines 20-24), run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, which executes fork-controlled lifecycle/postinstall scripts), and execute `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) — arbitrary attacker-authored code — on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18) with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (line 33) carrying `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` (lines 13-14). This is a classic 'pwn request': a fork PR can exfiltrate the token and compromise persistent self-hosted runner state.

findings.title: Don't silently override an explicitly configured 0ms grace duration
findings.whyItBreaks: 0 is a valid duration and setTimeout accepts it. Before this change, `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` produced RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 (SIGTERM then immediate SIGKILL on the next tick) and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` produced a 0ms give-up after SIGKILL. With `parsed > 0` those explicit zeros are now classified as invalid and silently replaced by the hardcoded fallbacks 5000 and 2000 at src/shared/runner-process.ts:3-10, so an operator who deliberately requested minimal teardown latency now waits an extra 5s (SIGKILL escalation) / 2s (give-up on escaped descendant) with no warning, and cannot distinguish 'unset' from 'set to 0'.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files get deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block built a `tail-coverage` hotspot from `bundle.changedFiles` not present in `hotspots` (the deleted comment: 'never silently skip a changed file'). It was the only guarantee that every changed file reaches a deep pass. `hotspots = sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (line 93) both drops changed files the map pass never assigned and truncates hotspots ranked 7th+, and the loop at line 97 now iterates only those survivors. Any changed file outside the selected hotspots is never sent to `runCodex(deepPrompt, ...)` and never appears in `all`, yet `reviewLarge` still returns a normal verdict/summary — a PASS can be issued for files that were never reviewed.

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual risks instead of hard-coding empty
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removed `const residuals: ResidualRisk[] = []`, `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)`, and replaced the field with `residual_risks: []`. `candidateMerged` is what is serialized into `{{FINDINGS}}` for the critic (line 116), and the returned `residualRisks`/`deriveVerdict` consume `pruned.residual_risks` (lines 122, 128). Because the candidate now always carries an empty residual list, any `blocks:true` residual emitted by a deep pass is discarded before the critic sees it; the final verdict can therefore report PASS while a deep pass explicitly said its hotspot could not be verified. This is a discarded failure/uncertainty signal (TRIGGER D).

findings.title: Restore per-hotspot failure isolation in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code wrapped the deep pass in try/catch, appending a 'DEEP PASS FAILED' checked entry and a `blocks:true` residual, then continuing the loop. It now calls `normalizeReview(extractJson(runCodex(...)))` unguarded inside the loop. A single malformed/empty codex response for any one hotspot (the very failure mode the explicit 'malformed output' checks elsewhere guard against) now throws out of reviewLarge, discarding the findings of all other successfully-completed hotspots and returning no ReviewResult at all — a reliability regression versus the prior honest partial result.

findings.title: formatDuration can render "1m 60s" when seconds round up
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is truncated with Math.floor while seconds is rounded independently, so a remainder in [59500, 59999] ms rounds to 60 and is never carried into minutes. For ms=119500: minutes=floor(119500/60000)=1, seconds=round((119500%60000)/1000)=round(59.5)=60, yielding the nonsensical "1m 60s"; for ms in [59500,59999] with minutes=0 it prints "60s". The previous code derived minutes and seconds from a single rounded totalSeconds, so seconds was always <60. This feeds the user-visible markdown stats line (src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80).

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger silently accepts 0 and empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported helper's name and thrown message promise a strictly positive integer, but `parsed < 0` lets zero through. `Number("")`, `Number(" ")`, and `Number("\n")` all evaluate to 0, so a missing/blank setting (unset env var, empty CLI arg) that previously raised `${label} requires a positive integer` is now returned as 0. Callers cannot distinguish "config missing/blank" or "explicit zero" from a valid positive value, so a zero silently flows into whatever the value sizes (timeout, attempts, count) with no error signal. Previously the same input hit the throw at base line 32; that failure signal is now downgraded to a legitimate-looking value.
